us-femaleA data center is a big building full of computers called servers . These servers store photos, emails, apps, and cloud services. Companies like Microsoft build very large data centers. People call them hyperscale data centers because they are so big. Servers get very hot when they work. So data centers need a lot of cooling . They also need cheap, clean power. For these reasons, companies often build them in cold places or near rivers and wind farms. A cold climate helps to keep the machines safe and saves money. Location is important for another reason: distance . When a data center is close to its users, the internet feels faster. This short delay is called latency . Low latency makes apps and video calls smooth and quick.

us-femaleMicrosoft started in 1975. For many years it was famous for Windows and Office . Today, a big part of its business is the cloud . Its cloud platform is called Azure . The cloud means that companies rent computers and storage online, instead of buying their own. Azure runs in data centers all over the world. Because of artificial intelligence (AI) , the world now needs much more computing power, so Microsoft is building new data centers very fast. These projects are huge. One single campus can cost billions of dollars and take years to build. Engineers, contract managers, and construction companies work together on tight deadlines . So a small delay in one date or one number can be very expensive.

us-femaleMany teams around the world start the day with a short meeting called a stand-up . The name comes from a simple idea: people stand up, so the meeting stays short. It usually lasts only ten or fifteen minutes. In a stand-up, each person answers three questions. What did I do yesterday? What will I do today? Is anything blocking me? On a construction site, a manager might ask, "Where do we stand on the raised floor?" and each coordinator gives a quick status update . This habit comes from software teams, but it works well on any project. It keeps everyone on the same page and helps the team find problems early, before they become big and expensive.

us-femaleA data center is a big building full of computers. These computers run the cloud and AI for companies like Microsoft. They must work all day and all night, with no stop. But what happens when the power goes down? The data center has a backup plan . First, big batteries called a UPS turn on in less than a second. They give power for a short time. Then, large generators start. They use fuel and can run for many hours. Because of this backup, the servers never stop. For the client, this is the safest choice, and on a construction site, the team must test it many times before the building opens.

us-femaleA good project manager cannot do everything alone. On a big site, like a Microsoft data center, there are many tasks every day. So the manager must delegate — this means to give a task to another person. Good delegation is clear. The leader says three things: who does the task, what the task is, and when it is due. For example: 'Ana, you are responsible for the safety report by Wednesday.' But delegation is not only about giving orders. The leader also offers help and checks the work later. This is called accountability . When people feel trusted, they work better, and the project moves faster.

us-femaleIn a data center , the design is very exact. Every cable, pipe, and cooling unit has a place. The client — for example, Microsoft — checks the plan and gives a sign-off . After that, the design is "approved." So why not change it later to save time? Because one small change can break many things. A new cable route may touch the power system or the cooling. It can also need a new test and a new sign-off from the client. That takes more time than it saves. This is why a contract manager often says "keep the approved design." It is not about being slow. It is about risk . A safe, boring choice protects the date, the budget, and the client's trust.

us-femaleA data center is a building full of computers. These computers run websites, apps, and cloud services. They must work all day and all night, every day. Even a short stop can be a big problem for the client. One common risk is heat. The computers get very hot, so the building needs cooling systems and water pipes. If a pipe breaks, there is a water leak . Water near electricity is dangerous. The team must stop work, shut off the water, and keep people away. Big companies plan for these moments. They have an emergency plan and a clear chain of command. One person takes charge and gives short, calm orders. Another person calls the client. A good plan turns a scary moment into a controlled one.
us-femaleThe bottom line is the client gets the data center on time.

us-femaleMany managers worry about one thing: their team members know more than they do. An electrical engineer knows more about power. A software engineer knows more about code. So how can you lead them? The secret is simple. A good leader does not need all the answers. A good leader asks the right questions and listens. When you say "What do you recommend?", you show respect. The expert feels valued, and you still guide the decision. This skill is very important in hyperscale projects, like the big data centers that companies such as Microsoft build. These projects need many specialists. The manager connects them, makes the final call, and takes the decision to the client. You lead with trust, not with technical answers.

us-femalePeople talk about the cloud every day. But the cloud is not in the sky. It is a network of very large buildings called data centers . Microsoft, Amazon, and Google own many of them around the world. Inside a data center there are thousands of computers, called servers . They store your photos, your emails, and your work files. When you open an app on your phone, a server in a data center does the job and sends the answer back to you in seconds. Microsoft's cloud is called Azure . Companies use Azure to run their software without buying their own machines. This is cheaper and faster for them. That is why so many new data centers are being built today.

us-femaleA tariff is a tax on goods that come from another country. When a country puts a tariff on imports, those products cost more. The buyer pays the extra money. This matters for big projects like data centers. Many parts — cooling units, steel, and chips — come from overseas . If a new tariff hits those parts, the price goes up. The whole supply chain feels it. For a contract manager, tariffs are a real concern . A price change can affect the budget and the schedule. This is why teams watch trade news and plan early. It is hard to control, but good planning helps.

us-femaleInside a big data center , the most important room is the data hall . This is the large open space where the servers live. The servers are the computers that store and process data for companies like Microsoft. A data hall needs three things all the time: power , cooling , and security . The servers use a lot of electricity, and they get very hot. So engineers install big cooling systems to keep the air cold. If the room gets too hot, the servers can stop working. Access to a data hall is controlled and slow. Workers often wait for permission to enter. In a construction contract, the date when a data hall is handed over to the client is very important. If the handover is late, the whole project can be delayed, and this can start a formal claim.

When you save a file in the cloud, it goes to a data center somewhere in the world. Microsoft runs a cloud service called Azure . Today, millions of companies use Azure every day. Because of this, Microsoft needs more and more space. So the company builds huge data centers in many countries, including Brazil. These new buildings use a lot of power and need strong cooling systems. The computers get very hot, so engineers must keep the rooms cold day and night. This is why teams check the cooling carefully and play it safe — better safe than sorry .

us-femaleA hyperscale data center is a very large building full of computers. Companies like Microsoft build them to run cloud services and AI . These projects are huge, and time is money. When a client signs a contract, both sides agree on key dates. These dates are called milestones . If the builder is late, the contract often has a penalty . This penalty is called liquidated damages . It is a fixed amount, often per day of delay. Why so strict? A data center makes money only when it is open. One day late can cost the client a lot. So the contract protects the client. But the rule is fair: the builder pays only if the delay is the builder's fault. A late design change from the client is a different story.

us-femaleBig construction projects use money tools to build trust. One common tool is a performance bond . It is a promise from a bank or an insurer. If the builder does not finish the work, the bank pays the client. The builder also needs insurance . Liability insurance covers damage to other people or property. All-risk insurance covers the site itself, for example a fire or a storm. These covers protect everyone if something goes wrong. For a Microsoft data center, the client wants proof. So the builder sends certificates . Each one shows the cover is valid and when it will expire . This paperwork is normal in the US market, and it makes the deal safe for both sides.
us-femaleThe key supplier delivers the cooling equipment.

us-femaleWhen a construction team finishes a building, they give it to the client. This step is called the handover . For a normal office, the handover is almost the end of the job. For a Microsoft data center, it is different. A data center is full of machines. The cooling system, the power system, and the backup generators must all work together. Before handover, engineers run many tests. This testing phase is called commissioning . They check every system, sometimes for weeks. The client does not accept the building until all the tests pass. At handover, the contractor gives the client the as-built documents . These papers show exactly how the building was made. They are very important, because the client needs them to run and repair the data center for many years. The warranty also starts at this moment. So the handover is a beginning, not just an end. The building starts its real life, and the servers go online.

us-femaleA big data center does not appear in one day. It follows a clear path with three main stages: design , build , and handover . Each stage has its own teams and its own goals. In the design phase , engineers plan everything on paper and on the computer. They draw the buildings, the power lines, and the cooling system. The client approves the design before any work starts on the land. Then comes the build phase . This is the loudest part. The civil team builds the structure, while the MEP team installs the electrical and mechanical systems. Often these works run in parallel to save time, because the cloud market moves fast and the client wants the servers online soon. Finally, after testing, the team reaches handover . The contractor gives the building to the client, and the data center starts its real job: keeping the cloud running, day and night.

These computers live in very large buildings called hyperscale data centers . A hyperscale data center has one owner and one big plan. Microsoft owns the building and uses all the space. This is different from a colocation site, where many companies rent space in the same building. Hyperscale means one company and a very large size. Why does Microsoft build so big? The answer is scale . When you use the same design again and again, you build faster and you save money. Microsoft builds the same kind of data center in many countries, so each new site is quick to plan and easy to run.

us-femaleBefore a data center goes up, engineers study the ground . A heavy building needs strong soil under it. If the soil is weak, the building can sink a little over time. This is called settlement , and it is a big problem. To check the ground, the team drills small holes called boreholes . They pull soil samples from different depths and send them to a lab. The lab measures how much weight the soil can hold. This number is the bearing capacity . Sometimes the soil is soft, or the water level is high. In this case, engineers use deep foundations . These long supports reach down to hard rock, so the heavy data center stays safe and level for many years.

us-femaleEvery large data center starts with a big question: should the building use steel or concrete ? Both are strong. Both are common. But they are good for different things. Steel is light and fast. Workers make the parts in a factory. Then they bring the parts to the site and put them together. This saves time. Steel is also good for large spans — big open rooms with no columns in the middle. Data halls need this open space for many servers. But steel can get weak in a fire, so builders must add fireproofing . Concrete is heavy and slow, but it is very strong and it resists fire well. The heavy mass also helps to stop vibration from big machines. Many teams now use a mix of both. This is called a hybrid system : a concrete core for safety, and a steel roof for speed and open space.

us-femaleImagine the same data center built in two countries: one in Texas and one in São Paulo. The drawings look almost the same, but the construction is not. Why? Because the rules and the costs are different. In the United States, workers are expensive, so companies want to build fast. They often use steel and precast concrete, made in a factory and lifted into place. Less time on site means less money on labor. In Brazil, the situation changes. There is a lot of skilled labor and it costs less. So cast-in-place concrete — poured right there on the site — is often cheaper and fits the local building code . This idea of changing a design to fit a new country is called tropicalization . The goal is the same building, but the smartest local solution.

us-femaleThe world needs more data centers, and it needs them fast. The boom in cloud and AI means companies like Microsoft want new buildings ready in months, not years. One key tool helps with this: prefabrication . With prefabrication, the steel columns and beams are made in a factory, called the shop. The work there is clean, dry, and well controlled. Then the parts come to the site ready to use. On site, the team only does the erection : a crane lifts each beam, and workers bolt the connections together. This way is faster and safer. There is less cutting and welding outdoors, so there are fewer accidents and fewer delays. Because the parts arrive ready, the project can stay ahead of schedule — and in the data center race, time is money.

us-femaleArizona is hot and dry. Phoenix can reach over a hundred degrees in summer. So why do big tech companies build data centers there? A data center is a large building full of computers that run the cloud and AI. The desert has good things for builders. The land is cheap and flat. The sky is clear, so solar power is easy. There are not many earthquakes or floods. Power lines are big and strong. Microsoft, Google, and other companies all build in Arizona. The heat is a problem for the servers, because computers make a lot of heat . The dry air helps. In dry air, water cools things fast by evaporation . New designs also use less water, because water is short in the desert. So Phoenix is now a big tech town. People say "howdy" on the job site, and the cranes work next to the cactus.

us-femaleComputers make heat . A big data center has thousands of servers, and they run all day and all night. If the room gets too hot, the servers fail. So cooling is one of the most important jobs in the building. The heat moves in steps. First, a cooling coil takes the heat from the air. The heat goes into cold water. Then chillers cool the water again. At the end, a cooling tower sends the heat outside. The water moves in a loop that never stops. Cooling uses a lot of power. In some data centers, cooling uses almost as much energy as the servers. So engineers work hard to make cooling more efficient . They also keep a pump and a chiller on standby, because the servers can never stop.
us-femaleThe cooling towers reject the heat. → The heat is rejected by the cooling towers.
us-femaleWhen free cooling is used, the chillers are not run.

us-femaleData centers use a lot of water . Many of them cool their servers with cooling towers . In a cooling tower, water gets warm and then turns into vapor. This is called evaporation , and it pulls heat out of the system. But the water that evaporates is gone, so the tower needs new water all the time. This new water is called makeup water . One large data center can use millions of liters of water in a year. In dry places like Arizona, this is a problem, because water is short there. People who live near the site sometimes worry about it. So companies look for better ways. On cool days, they use free cooling : the outside air is cold, so the chillers can rest and the towers use less water. Some new designs use air cooling or special liquids, so that they need almost no water at all. Water and power are now part of every big contract. A construction manager must understand them, because the client asks about them on every visit.

us-femaleInside a data center, thousands of servers run all day and all night. They do a lot of work, and they make a lot of heat . If the heat stays in the room, the servers get too hot and stop working. So keeping the room cool is one of the most important jobs. Engineers use a simple idea: keep the cold air and the hot air apart. Cold air goes to the front of the racks. The servers pull it in. Hot air comes out the back. A wall or a ceiling, called containment , stops the two from mixing. When they do not mix, the cooling is much more efficient. This matters for money too. Cooling can use a big part of a data center's power. When companies like Microsoft cool better, they save energy and they spend less. Good airflow is not only good engineering — it is good business.

us-femaleA big data center uses a huge amount of power — as much as a small town. The power comes a long way, from the grid to the rack. On that trip, engineers move it in medium voltage first. Why? Higher voltage means less loss . When power travels at a higher voltage, less energy turns into heat in the cables. So the site moves power across the building in medium voltage, and the engineers waste less. Near the servers, a transformer steps the power down to low voltage . The equipment runs on low voltage, because that is what it is built for. The idea is simple: medium voltage moves the power, and low voltage uses it. This small rule helps Microsoft run thousands of servers without losing energy on the way.

us-femaleA big data center cannot stop. If the servers lose power for even one second, websites, banks, and apps can go down. So engineers build many layers of backup power. They want the building to keep running, no matter what happens outside. The first layer is the UPS . It uses batteries. When the city power fails, the UPS holds the load for a few minutes. But batteries are small. They cannot run the building for hours. That is the job of the generators . The generators run on diesel fuel. They start in seconds and can carry the full load for many hours. The site keeps large fuel tanks, and trucks bring more diesel when needed. Engineers also test the generators with a fake load, called a load bank , to be sure they work before a real emergency.
us-femaleIf the cooling fails, we will switch to the backup unit.

us-femaleFor many years, big tech companies built data centers for normal cloud work, like email and storage. But now there is a new and very strong reason to build more: artificial intelligence . AI models need a huge amount of computing power, and that power lives inside data centers. Companies like Microsoft , Amazon, and Google are spending billions of dollars on new sites. These are not small buildings. A modern hyperscale data center can be as big as many football fields, and it uses as much electricity as a small city. This boom is good news for construction and engineering firms. There is a lot of work, but also pressure, because the clients want the buildings ready fast. A company that can build well and on time, like Racional, has a strong place in this growing market.

us-femaleOn a small job, a worker can remember where every cable goes. On a data center, with thousands of cables, no one can. This is why documentation matters so much. A clear label at both ends of a cable is a small thing, but it saves hours of work later. This habit is also a soft skill. Clients like Microsoft trust teams that are organized and careful. When you label, record, and report well, the client sees that the project is under control. Being clear and consistent is part of being professional, not only on cables, but in emails and contracts too.
us-femaleThe backup tank (that) we installed feeds the fire water supply.

us-femaleIn most buildings, a fire is fought with water. But inside a data center, water is the enemy. The servers run on electricity, and a single drop in the wrong place can destroy expensive hardware and erase data. So engineers protect these mission-critical rooms in a very different way. The first line of defense is detection. Tiny tubes constantly pull air from the room and send it to a sensor. This is called air-sampling smoke detection, and it can find a problem long before a human would smell smoke. Because it reacts so early, the team often has time to fix the issue before a real fire starts. If the fire grows, the room uses a clean agent instead of water. This is a special gas that removes heat or oxygen so that the flames stop, but it does not wet or damage the equipment. The gas is stored under pressure and discharges in seconds. Meanwhile, support areas around the data hall still use sprinklers, because there the cost of water is lower than the cost of fire.

us-femaleA few years ago, most people had never heard the words hyperscale data center . Today they are some of the largest and most expensive buildings on the planet. The reason is simple: the world suddenly wants much more computing power , and that power has to live somewhere. The main driver is the AI boom . Every time a company trains a new model, it needs thousands of powerful chips running day and night. These chips produce a lot of heat and use enormous amounts of electricity, so they cannot sit in a normal office. They need a purpose-built facility with advanced cooling, backup power, and tight security. As a result, the big players such as Microsoft, Amazon, and Google are investing hundreds of billions of dollars in new sites around the world. This trend has changed the construction industry. A project that once took years of planning now has to be delivered as fast as possible, because demand keeps growing. Teams in different countries build similar designs at the same time, so that capacity comes online quickly. For an engineer or a contract manager, it is an exciting time, but also a demanding one. For Brazil, the wave is just arriving. Local companies that learn to build to this global standard now will be in the front line of one of the biggest construction markets of the decade.

us-femaleFor years, building a data center was mostly a question of money and land. Today it is also a question of supply chain . Because so many companies want to train artificial intelligence at the same time, the demand for critical equipment has exploded. The hardest items to get are power equipment and high-capacity transformers, and some of them now have a lead time of two years or more. This matters for the people who manage vendors. A few years ago, a contract manager could order a generator or a cooling unit and expect it within months. Now the order must be placed very early, sometimes before the building design is even final, so that the milestone is not put at risk. As a result, the relationship with suppliers like Eaton, Schneider, Cummins, and Vertiv has become more strategic, not just transactional. Hyperscale clients such as Microsoft understand this well. They often pre-approve vendors and even reserve production slots in advance, because a delay on one critical package can stop a whole project. So the modern job is less about finding the cheapest price and more about protecting the schedule and managing the relationship over time.

us-femaleData centers use a huge amount of power , and they use it twenty-four hours a day. A single hyperscale site can use as much electricity as a small city. Because the AI boom needs even more computing, companies like Microsoft, Google and Amazon now worry that the grid cannot give them enough clean, steady energy. This is why Big Tech is looking again at nuclear power . In 2024, Microsoft signed a deal to restart a reactor at Three Mile Island, the famous US plant. Other companies are funding small modular reactors (SMRs) , which are smaller and faster to build than a traditional plant. Nuclear is attractive because it runs around the clock and produces almost no carbon. However, nuclear is not the only answer. Solar power is cheap and clean, but it stops at night, so it needs batteries. Natural gas is flexible and can cover the peaks in demand, but it is not low-carbon. For this reason, most sites use an energy mix : solar by day, gas or batteries for backup, and, in the future, nuclear for the steady base load.
us-femaleThe cooling works are running ahead of schedule.

us-femaleEvery large project has many tasks, and some of them depend on others. The critical path is the longest chain of dependent tasks — the one that decides the project's end date. If any task on the critical path is late, the whole project is late. Tasks that are not on it have some float , which means they can slip a little without causing a delay . The method is older than most people think. The critical path method was developed in the late 1950s by the US company DuPont to manage complex industrial projects. Because it worked so well, it spread to construction, software and, today, to building hyperscale data centers . On a modern site, the critical path can change every week. This week it may run through the electrical room; next week, after the inspections, it may move to the cooling system. So good managers do not just build the schedule once — they track it daily and protect the tasks with zero float , because those are the ones that can break the milestone .
us-femaleThe cooling package came in under budget.

us-femaleBuilding a hyperscale data center is one of the most expensive projects in modern construction. A single Microsoft Azure campus can cost several billion dollars, so forecasting the cost-at-completion is critical. However, these budgets are difficult to predict because the technology inside the building changes very fast. One big challenge is the equipment. The price of chips and cooling systems can move quickly, and the AI boom has pushed demand even higher. Because of this, the cost to complete a project can shift between the design phase and the day the servers are installed. Managers must update their forecast often, so that the client is never surprised. Another challenge is power. Data centers need huge amounts of electricity, and connecting to the grid can be slow and expensive. If a power upgrade is delayed, the schedule slips and costs rise. For this reason, good contract managers track both the cost to date and the cost to complete every single month. The lesson is simple but powerful: a forecast is not a promise, it is a living number. The best teams report small savings rather than a late surprise, because trust is built on honest projections.

us-femaleCooling is at L4.

us-femaleBuilding a hyperscale data center is only half the job. Before a single server goes live, the whole facility must pass commissioning — a series of tests that prove every system works as designed. Power, cooling, fire protection and controls are all checked, because a failure after launch could cost a cloud provider millions of dollars per hour. The tests run in levels, often called L1 to L5. The early levels look at single pieces of equipment, while the final level, the integrated systems test , runs everything together and even simulates a real failure, such as a power cut. The team watches to see whether the backup generators start fast enough so that the servers never lose power. This matters more than ever because of the AI boom. Companies like Microsoft are racing to open new capacity, however they will not switch on a site until commissioning is signed off. A clean commissioning report is what gives the client the confidence to migrate live workloads onto the new building.
us-femaleThe goal is a carbon neutral data center.
us-femaleWe cut water use so that the cooling stays efficient.

us-femaleData centers use a huge amount of energy and water, mostly to keep thousands of servers cool. As the AI boom grows, this footprint grows too, so big tech companies are under pressure to build cleaner sites. Many now target green building standards such as LEED , which rewards efficient design, recycled materials and low water use. One key number is PUE , or Power Usage Effectiveness. It compares the total energy a site uses with the energy that actually reaches the servers. A perfect score is 1.0, and modern hyperscale sites push close to it, because every wasted watt costs money and adds carbon. Water is now just as important as power. Older sites used millions of liters for cooling, however newer designs reuse water or switch to air cooling so that local supplies are protected. Microsoft, for example, has promised to become water positive , meaning it plans to return more water than it consumes. For a builder, this changes the job on site. Teams must recycle construction waste, source renewable energy and track results every week, because the client checks these targets before granting final acceptance.

us-femaleWhen José Mário opens his first meeting with the Microsoft team, the very first minutes are about people, not the project. In US corporate culture, a first meeting usually starts with a few seconds of small talk — a friendly question about the weekend, the trip, or even the weather. This may feel like a waste of time, however it is used to break the ice and to make everyone comfortable before the real work begins. The self-introduction that follows is kept short and clear. Americans like a quick line that says who you are and what you do, so a strong opening is something like "I'm José Mário, the contract manager from Racional, and I'll be your main point of contact on the data center project." Because the relationship is new, a confident handshake or a warm smile on camera is appreciated, and first names are used almost immediately, even with senior people. Good meeting etiquette also means a few simple habits. Arrive a couple of minutes early, turn your camera on for a remote call, and let the host open the agenda. When you are introduced to the hyperscale data center stakeholders, listen for their roles so that later you know who decides what. This light, respectful start builds trust that will help every difficult conversation later in the project.

us-femaleWhen José Mário lands in Texas for a business trip , he is arriving in one of the busiest construction regions in the United States. Over the last decade, Texas has become a leading home for hyperscale data centers — the giant buildings that power cloud services like Microsoft Azure. Companies chose the state because land is wide and relatively cheap, taxes are low, and the local government welcomes large industrial projects. Energy is the other big reason. Data centers need a huge amount of electricity, so they look for places with strong power supply. Texas runs its own electric grid and has a fast-growing mix of natural gas, wind, and solar power. However, the recent AI boom has pushed demand so high that even Texas now worries about whether it can build enough power lines in time. For an engineer or a contract manager, a trip to a Texas site is also a cultural experience. American colleagues often mix business with casual talk, so after a long day they may invite you to grab dinner and chat about anything but work. Accepting these invitations is a smart way to build trust, because much of the real relationship is formed outside the meeting room.
